Brownsville by the numbers

Which offices value and bill a Brownsville house?

Cameron Appraisal District staff set the value, and the Cameron County Tax Assessor-Collector mails a single combined bill. That office also collects for the county, the schools, the cities and the special districts inside Cameron County, which means one payment covers every unit. Write to it at P.O. Box 952, Brownsville, TX 78522-0920, or call (956) 544-0800.

The appraisal district points out that people often confuse it with the tax office. It has no tax amounts and takes no payments, so bill questions go to the assessor-collector. The district keeps longer hours early in the week, 7:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. Monday through Thursday and 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Friday, and its website has a property search and a map search.

No state property tax exists in Texas, the Comptroller confirms, and each local unit picks its own rate. A house just across a school district line can therefore carry a noticeably different bill.

Which taxing units tax a Brownsville home, and at what 2026 rates?

For the 2026 tax year, the City of Brownsville adopted a rate of $0.603504 per $100 of taxable value, the same figure it adopted for 2025 and 2024. The table lists the units that levy on most Brownsville homes, as printed in the county's Truth in Taxation summary.

Taxing unit2026 adopted rate per $1002025 adopted rate per $100
City of Brownsville$0.603504$0.603504
Brownsville ISD$0.771600$0.831460
Cameron County$0.424393$0.424393

Brownsville Navigation District$0.025589$0.025589

Source: Cameron County, Truth in Taxation Summary.

The same table breaks the 2026 city rate into $0.353581 for maintenance and operations and $0.249923 for debt. Its no-new-revenue rate is $0.563407 and its voter-approval rate is $0.613440.

  • 2022 city rate: $0.691919
  • 2023 city rate: $0.607987, which the city's own notice described as a 12.13 percent drop from the year before
  • Brownsville ISD in 2022: $1.208690, compared with $0.771600 for 2026

Properties in a drainage district, municipal utility district or other special district pay an added levy, so check your bill for every line.

What are the due date and the late penalties for a Brownsville tax bill?

The collector mails bills around October 1, and payment is due by January 31. Taxes unpaid on February 1 are delinquent, and the Comptroller says a six percent penalty and one percent interest are added at that point. Cameron County's tax office describes the same hit as 7 percent penalty and interest on balances left after the deadline.

The penalty then rises one percent a month, and on July 1 it becomes 12 percent, with interest still growing at one percent a month. A unit that hires a private attorney can add up to 20 percent more. An owner can request a waiver of penalty and interest under Tax Code 33.011, which generally requires paying within 21 days of learning the bill was late.

The Cameron tax office offers a quarter pay plan for owners who are 65 or older, disabled, or a disabled veteran or surviving spouse of one, who claim a homestead:

  • First installment by January 31
  • Second installment by March 31
  • Third installment by May 31
  • Final installment by July 31

Online payment fees are posted by the office: $1.00 for an internet check of $5,000 or less, $3.00 for larger checks, and a 3 percent convenience fee on credit and debit cards.

What property tax relief can Brownsville homeowners claim?

The largest break is the residence homestead exemption. School districts must exempt $140,000 of a home's value, and owners aged 65 and up or with a disability receive $60,000 more against school taxes. The state also limits a homestead's yearly appraisal increase to 10 percent, and it holds the school tax on a senior's or disabled owner's home at the first qualifying amount.

A newer local option comes from the Brownsville Navigation District, known as the Port of Brownsville. In September 2026 the city posted that the district approved a 100 percent homestead exemption for qualifying homeowners who are 65 or older or have a qualifying disability, covering Brownsville, Rancho Viejo, Los Fresnos, Indian Lake and Starbase. It starts with the 2027 tax year, and owners apply through the appraisal district.

Disabled veterans may qualify for partial exemptions on a sliding scale, and a veteran with a 100 percent rating gets a full exemption on the homestead. File exemption applications with the appraisal district by April 30, using Form 50-114 for the homestead exemptions. Owners who inherit a home and are not on a recorded deed must supply an affidavit, a death certificate and a recent utility bill.

How do I protest a Brownsville appraisal?

A written protest goes to the appraisal review board by May 15 or 30 days after the value notice arrives, whichever is later. Hearings start around May 15, per the Comptroller, and homestead notices are mailed on or about April 1.

If the board's ruling is not satisfactory, there are three further paths: district court, binding arbitration, or an appeal to the State Office of Administrative Hearings when the board's value is over $1,000,000. Anyone appealing must still pay the undisputed tax before the delinquency date, or the appeal can be lost.

Bring evidence to the hearing, such as recent sales of similar houses nearby, repair estimates and photos of defects. Ask the Cameron Appraisal District for its protest forms and hearing schedule when you file.

What is Brownsville like as a place to own a home?

Brownsville sits at the southernmost tip of Texas, facing Matamoros across the Rio Grande, and serves as the Cameron County seat. The Handbook of Texas traces the town to 1848, when Charles Stillman and a partner laid out a townsite next to Fort Brown. Brownsville became county seat on January 13, 1849, and the Brownsville Navigation District, which still levies a tax, was voted in during December 1928 to build the ship channel. The Port of Brownsville opened on May 15, 1936.

The University of Texas at Brownsville partnered with Texas Southmost College beginning in 1991, and the college district still has its own tax line. U.S. 77 and U.S. 83 end here, and Brownsville is a major port of entry to Mexico.

  • Mid-2025 estimate: 192,957 residents, 3.6 percent above the 2020 base
  • Typical owned home, 2020 to 2024 survey: valued at $139,900
  • Share of homes lived in by their owners: 61.7 percent
  • Typical monthly rent: $923, with 3.13 people per household
  • Land area: 131.53 square miles

All five come from the QuickFacts column for Brownsville city.

Can a Brownsville house with unpaid tax still be sold?

Yes, because the title company asks the tax office for a payoff figure and settles the balance when the sale funds. The lien that attaches each January 1 secures that year's bill, and the January 1 owner stays personally liable for it after any later sale.

If the bill is already delinquent, ask the Cameron County tax office about a payment agreement. The Comptroller says some collectors allow up to 36 months on delinquent taxes, and that a plan is required for a residence homestead. Once a collection suit starts, court costs are added to the bill.

Tax foreclosure sales are public auctions, usually run by the constable or an agent for the taxing unit, and there is no statewide list. Check the Cameron County clerk and tax office sites for sale notices.

More questions about Brownsville, TX Property Tax Guide

What city rate applies to a Brownsville home for 2026?

The city adopted $0.603504 per $100 of taxable value, unchanged from 2025 and 2024. It is only the city's slice of the total bill.

On what date does a Brownsville tax bill go delinquent?

February 1 is the delinquency date for a bill left unpaid after January 31. A six percent penalty and one percent interest attach then, and the penalty climbs until it hits 12 percent on July 1.

Where does a Brownsville owner send the property tax payment?

To the Cameron County Tax Assessor-Collector, which bills and collects for the county, school district, city and special districts. The appraisal district takes no payments.

Do older Brownsville homeowners get extra exemptions?

Yes. Schools add $60,000 for owners 65 and up or disabled, on top of the $140,000 homestead exemption, and the Brownsville Navigation District approved a full exemption for them starting with the 2027 tax year.

What is the deadline to dispute a Brownsville appraisal?

May 15 or 30 days after the notice is delivered, whichever comes later. Send the written notice to the appraisal review board through the Cameron Appraisal District.

The City Council adopted $0.537000 per $100 of assessed value for fiscal year 2027, which began October 1. A city news release calls it the lowest rate since 1989 and the 13th straight annual cut, down from $0.537500. The city also kept its senior and disabled exemptions at $110,000.

Three school districts are listed for Carrollton: Carrollton-Farmers Branch, Lewisville and Dallas ISD. Collin County's rate is not on that table, so ask the Denton County Tax Office or the Collin Central Appraisal District if your house is on the Collin side.

Where do Carrollton property tax dollars go?

For the average Carrollton homestead, the city's taxation page splits each dollar of property tax this way: $0.59 to the school district, $0.30 to the city and $0.11 to the county. The school share funds schools and operations. The city share pays for police, fire, streets, the library, parks, development, environmental work and animal control, and the county share covers county roads, sheriff services, courts and health and human services.

The city's finance page adds that the tax rate has two parts, maintenance and operations plus debt, and that the Council sets the rate with the budget in August. A separate stormwater fee began October 1, 2026 on utility bills. The release says about 80 percent of residential properties land in Tier 2 at $7.25. It is a utility charge, not a property tax.

When are Carrollton property taxes due, and what are the penalties?

Taxes become payable October 1 and turn delinquent if unpaid by January 31. The city page lists the late charges in plain terms:

  • A 6% penalty on the first day of the month of delinquency, rising 1% a month until July 1, when it becomes 12%
  • Interest of 1% at the start, then 1% more each month
  • An added penalty of up to 20% of taxes, penalties and interest if the tax is still unpaid on July 1

The Texas Comptroller describes a split payment option: half by November 30 and half by June 30, and a waiver of penalty and interest requested in writing within the window it explains. Homeowners 65 or older or disabled may also pay in four installments. Ask the county tax office to confirm which option you qualify for before you rely on it.

Pay the county office that bills your parcel. The city page lists mail, online and in-person choices for each office.

  • Dallas County parcels: mail to the Dallas County Tax Assessor-Collector, 500 Elm St., Dallas, TX 75202, or pay in person at the North Dallas location, 6820 LBJ Freeway, Suite 1300, Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Phone 214-653-7811.
  • Denton and Collin parcels: mail to the Denton County Tax Assessor-Collector, 1505 E. McKinney Street, Denton, TX 76209-4525, or pay in person at the Carrollton location, 1029 W. Rosemeade Parkway, Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Phone 940-349-3500.
  • Online payments carry fees, and both offices accept cards and echeck.

File for every exemption you qualify for, and protest the value if you think it is too high. The city offers a 20 percent homestead exemption, a $110,000 exemption for owners 65 or older, a $110,000 exemption for disabled persons and a disabled veterans exemption. You file with the appraisal district, never with the city. The city page says exemptions filed by May 1 appear on the original statement, and later filings produce a supplemental bill.

On the school side, the Comptroller says school districts must give a $140,000 residence homestead exemption, plus $60,000 more for homeowners 65 or older or disabled. For a protest, the deadline calendar sets May 15, or the 30th day after delivery of the notice when that is later. The city page says appraisal notices usually arrive in April and that the appraisal district, not the city, hears the case.

Who owes this year's tax if I sell my Carrollton house?

The Comptroller says value and ownership are fixed as of January 1, and its calendar says the tax lien attaches on that date. The bill for the year then arrives in October, after many spring and summer sales have closed. Ask the closing agent how the year's tax will be split between you and the buyer.

If you owe back taxes, the penalties in the schedule above keep growing until July 1. Ask the title company for a payoff figure from the county tax office rather than estimating, and do not rely on a number from a prior year's statement.

Carrollton packs a large population into a small footprint. Census QuickFacts lists these figures:

  • Land area: 36.66 square miles, or 3,640.2 people per square mile in 2020
  • Owner-occupied rate: 58.5%, across 51,995 households
  • Median owner-occupied home value: $381,000 for 2020 to 2024
  • Median gross rent: $1,735; median household income: $101,396
  • Foreign-born residents: 28.0%; mean commute: 24.1 minutes

The Census figure is a survey median and the city's figure is an average of homestead market values, so the two will not match.

$0.537000 per $100 of assessed value, lowered from $0.537500. The city calls it the lowest rate since 1989. School, county and special district rates are added on top of the city's.

After January 31. Taxes are payable from October 1, and a 6% penalty plus 1% interest start the month after the deadline. The penalty reaches 12% on July 1.

No. The Dallas, Denton and Collin central appraisal districts hear protests and approve exemptions. File by May 15 or within 30 days of delivery of the appraisal notice, whichever is later.
